formNote: Add 기 to a verb stem, then use 시작하다 to mark the beginning of an action.
usage: When I start exercising I feel good.
examples: These days I started reading books.
mistakes: Do not attach 기 to a noun directly.

formNote: Add 게 되다 to a verb stem to show a change of state caused by outside circumstances.
usage: I ended up living in Korea.
I came to like that person.
I ended up quitting the company.
I came to eat spicy food.
examples: How did you come to learn Korean?
I ended up taking that task.
mistakes: Do not use it for clear personal decisions.

formNote: Add 아 있다 or 어 있다 to a verb stem to show a resulting state that stays after the action.
usage: I am sitting on a chair.
examples: The picture is hanging on the wall.
mistakes: Do not use it with action verbs like 먹다.

formNote: Add ㄹ 때 after a vowel stem or 을 때 after a consonant stem to mean the time when something happens.
usage: When I eat, I drink water.
When I go home, I call.
When I am tired, I rest.
When I was young, I lived in Busan.
examples: When I study, I listen to music.
When the weather is nice, I walk.
When I feel bad, I sleep.
mistakes: Do not forget 을 after consonant stems.

formNote: Add 는 동안 to a verb stem to show that two actions happen over the same stretch of time.
usage: While I study, I turn off the phone.
While I work, I drink coffee.
examples: While I wait, I read a book.
While traveling, I took many photos.
While the baby sleeps, I clean.
mistakes: Do not use 은 동안 with verbs.

formNote: Add 지만 directly to a verb or adjective stem to connect two contrasting ideas in one sentence.
usage: It is raining but I go out.
I am hungry but I endure.
I am busy but I exercise.
examples: These clothes are expensive but pretty.
I am a student but I also work.
I am tired but I study.
mistakes: Do not add tense before 지만 usually.

formNote: Add 거나 to a verb stem to list two or more actions as alternative choices you can pick from.
usage: On weekends I sleep or watch movies.
I drink coffee or drink tea.
I take the bus or walk.
I read books or listen to music.
examples: I rest or take a walk.
I call or send a text.
mistakes: Do not use 거나 to connect two nouns.

formNote: Add 마다 to a noun to mean each one or every time, showing something repeats without exception.
usage: Every country has a different culture.
examples: I go to Busan every year.
mistakes: Do not attach 마다 to a verb stem.

formNote: Add 자마자 to a verb stem to show the second action happens right after the first one finishes.
usage: As soon as I get home, I wash my hands.
As soon as I wake up, I drink water.
As soon as class ends, I go home.
As soon as I ate, I slept.
examples: As soon as I arrive, I call.
I knew it as soon as I saw it.
As soon as I heard, I laughed.
mistakes: Do not add tense before 자마자.

formNote: Add 려면 after a vowel stem or 으려면 after a consonant stem to mean if you plan to do something.
usage: If you intend to be good at Korean, practice daily.
If you want to be healthy, you must sleep well.
If you intend to read, you need glasses.
If you intend to catch the train, hurry.
examples: If you intend to lose weight, exercise.
If you intend to succeed, you must try.
If you intend to buy a house, save money.
mistakes: Do not forget 으 after consonant stems.
